newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL overnight rate drops sharply on fall in swaps.
newsitem.headline: KL overnight rate drops sharply on fall in swaps.

text.p: The overnight interbank rate fell to 7.5/8.5 percent at 0800 GMT on Monday against 18/20 percent on Friday due to an increase in domestic market liquidity, dealers said on Monday.
They said more ringgit funds were coming back to the system through swaps, which was pulling down domestic short-term rates.
Dealers said foreign investors were seen lending ringgit heavily earlier in the afternoon, but why they were doing so was not clear.
"There is a fresh inflow into the system. It could be an intervention by the central bank, but we cannot confirm that," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
Some other dealers from large local banks said Bank Negara was probably intervening through one or two of its agents, who are also its principal dealers.
No independent confirmation could be obtained as Bank Negara does not comment on its market intervention operations.
The dealers said Bank Negara was believed to be in the market lending one-month money at the 8.5 percent level.
Earlier, other interbank rates were steady on increased bidding by local banks covering their positions on fears that the tightness in the domestic market would continue.
"Realising that this situation (of tightness) is not likely to go away very soon, the local banks are covering their positions," said a senior dealer at a Malaysian bank.
The one-week interbank rate at 11.0 percent and two-week at 9.0/11 percent, were both unchanged from Friday.
One-month money at 8.5/9.0 percent and three-month and six-month at 7.5/9.0 percent, were also steady.

The rise in interbank rates started 10 days ago, after Bank Negara intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market to stem the slide of the ringgit. The central bank was said to have sold around $1 billion.
The intervention drained liquidity from the system, causing the market to be short, and interbank rates to rise to unusually high levels, dealers said.
Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange reversed morning trend and were trading higher due to a shift in the sentiment of the cash market, futures dealers said.
At 0815 GMT, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) contract for June 1997 was up one point at 92.52, or an implied yield of 7.48 percent.
September 1997 contract was up two points at 92.62, or 7.38 percent and December was up eight at 92.68, or 7.32 percent.
